title: How Glaciers Shape the Land
subject: geo
paras: A glacier is a large mass of ice that moves slowly over land. Glaciers form in places where more snow falls in winter than melts in summer. Year after year, the snow builds up and is pressed into dense ice by the weight of the layers above it. When the ice becomes thick enough, usually several tens of meters, it begins to flow under its own weight, much like extremely thick syrup.

As glaciers move, they act as powerful agents of erosion. Ice itself is softer than most rock, but glaciers carry rocks and sand frozen into their base. Dragged along the ground, this material works like sandpaper, scratching and polishing the bedrock. Geologists can still see these long scratches, called striations, on rocks in places where glaciers disappeared thousands of years ago, and the direction of the scratches reveals which way the ice moved.

Glaciers also remove rock through a process called plucking. Meltwater seeps into cracks in the bedrock beneath the glacier and refreezes, attaching the rock to the ice. When the glacier moves forward, it pulls the loosened blocks away. Over long periods, plucking and scraping together can carve whole valleys. River valleys typically have a V shape, but valleys shaped by glaciers are U-shaped, with steep walls and broad, flat floors. Yosemite Valley in California is a famous example.

Everything a glacier removes must eventually be deposited somewhere. When the ice melts, it drops an unsorted mixture of clay, sand, gravel, and boulders known as till. Ridges of till left at the edges or front of a glacier are called moraines. Some boulders carried by ice end up far from where they started; these erratics may sit alone in a field, made of a type of rock found nowhere nearby.

Glacial landscapes help scientists reconstruct the history of Earth's climate. During the last ice age, which ended about 11,700 years ago, ice sheets covered much of North America and northern Europe. The Great Lakes, the fjords of Norway, and many hills in New England are all products of this ice. By mapping moraines and erratics, researchers can determine how far the ice once reached.

qs.q: According to paragraph 1, glaciers form in places where
opts: summers are very hot
more snow falls than melts each year
rivers freeze in winter
the ground is mostly flat
qs.why: more snow falls in winter than melts in summer。

qs.q: Why does the author mention "sandpaper" in paragraph 2?
opts: To explain how rocks in the ice wear down the bedrock
To show that glaciers contain sand
To describe how people study glaciers
To compare the color of ice and sand
qs.why: 冰底的岩石像砂纸一样刮擦、磨光基岩。

qs.q: The word "reveals" in paragraph 2 is closest in meaning to
opts: hides
shows
changes
doubles

qs.q: According to paragraph 3, how does plucking remove rock?
opts: Wind blows rock off the glacier surface.
Water freezes in cracks, attaching rock to the ice, which then pulls it away.
Rivers carry rock downhill.
Heat from the sun splits the rock.
qs.why: Meltwater seeps into cracks… refreezes… pulls the loosened blocks away。

qs.q: Based on paragraph 3, a geologist who finds a valley with steep walls and a wide, flat floor would most likely conclude that
opts: a river formed it
a glacier once shaped it
it is very young
it was made by people
qs.why: U 形谷是冰川作用的特征。

qs.q: According to paragraph 4, what makes a boulder an erratic?
opts: It is the largest rock in a moraine.
It was carried by ice far from where it formed.
It is made of clay and sand.
It has striations on it.
qs.why: carried by ice… far from where they started… found nowhere nearby。

qs.q: According to paragraph 5, all of the following were shaped by ice-age glaciers EXCEPT
opts: the Great Lakes
the fjords of Norway
hills in New England
the V-shaped river valleys
qs.why: V 形谷是河流形成的（第3段）。

qs.q: Select THREE answer choices that express the most important ideas of the passage. Introductory sentence: Glaciers are powerful forces that reshape the land.
opts: Glaciers erode bedrock by scraping it with embedded rock and by plucking blocks away.
Glacial erosion produces distinctive U-shaped valleys.
Yosemite Valley is located in California.
Material dropped by melting glaciers forms till, moraines, and erratics that record the ice's extent.
Ice is softer than most rock.
Syrup flows more slowly than water.
